chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Mahbub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

Indeed, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) raised his head towards the sky and smiled. So it was said to him: 'O Messenger of God! We saw you raise your head towards the sky and smile.' He said: 'Yes.

I was astounded at two angels who had descended from the sky to the earth, seeking a righteous believing servant in a prayer place where he used to pray, in order to record his deeds for his day and his night. But they did not find him in his prayer place, so they ascended to the sky.

And they said: 'Our Lord! Your believing servant, so-and-so — we sought him in his prayer place to record his deeds for his day and his night, but we did not find him, and we found him in Your ropes (held by illness).'

So God, Mighty and Majestic, said: 'Record for My servant the likes of what he used to do in his well-being, from the goodness during his day and his night, for as long as he remains in My ropes; for it is upon Me to record for him the reward of what he used to do in his well-being, when I have held him back from it.'

key_terms.حِبَالِي: My ropes — a metaphor for illness or affliction that binds and restrains a person from their normal deeds
key_terms.صِحَّة: Well-being, health — the state in which a person is able to perform their habitual acts of worship
key_terms.عَمَلَهُ: His deeds — specifically the habitual righteous acts the believer regularly performed before falling ill
key_terms.مُصَلًّى: Prayer mat or designated place of prayer — a space that a devout Muslim regularly returns to for worship

ai.seo_question: Does a sick Muslim still receive reward for acts of worship they are unable to perform due to illness?
ai.summary: This hadith narrates that the Prophet Muhammad (SAWW) was moved to smile upon witnessing two recording angels who had descended to document a righteous believer's deeds, only to find him bedridden with illness. God's direct command to write full reward for the sick man reveals a profound theological principle: a sincere believer's intention and habitual practice of worship are credited even when physical incapacity prevents their fulfillment. The phrase 'in My ropes' (فِي حِبَالِي) uses the metaphor of being bound — illness as divine captivity — to emphasize that God Himself is the one who prevents the servant, thus God guarantees the continuity of reward. This teaching would have deeply comforted early Muslim communities where illness and hardship were common, assuring them that sincere devotion is never lost.
